review.publication: Local only. No commit, push or deployment.
review.scope: Kitchen utensils and cookware, food-processing purposes, measurement tools, household cleaning, and selected malformed action terms.
review.attribution: Reviewed adaptations of Open English WordNet 2025 by the Open English WordNet Team, derived from Princeton WordNet. Retain CC BY 4.0 and underlying Princeton notices in docs/quality/2026-10-09-q11.md#sources-and-reuse. Manufacturer documentation, the Corning Museum of Glass collection and Gramota dictionary evidence refine selected scopes; no marketing, care or safety advice is imported.
review.context_policy: All new assertions use U1 and unspecified strength. Existing contexts, relation grammar and explicit negations remain unchanged. Unsupported inherited material percentages are rejected without inventing replacement prevalence estimates.

sense_decisions.scope: Preparing food through applied heat, narrower than the existing general food-preparation branch.
Cooking vessels and pans intended for heating food. Restrict the broad dictionary cooking-utensil cluster; a food turner or whisk is not a vessel.
Cookware intended for baking or roasting in an oven; no single material, temperature limit or food product is asserted.
A deep cooking vessel with a projecting handle, selected within the broad cooking-pot family. Not an excavator bucket.
A cooking pot intended for preparing stock. No fixed volume or material is asserted.
A frying pan whose pan body is cast iron; coatings and handles may use other materials.
A frying pan with an aluminum body; induction plates, coatings or handles need not be aluminum.
A cooking pot with a glass body. The museum saucepan is evidence of the material possibility, not a universal handle, stove-compatibility or care rule.
A spoon intended for eating. Move the overly broad eating-purpose assertion here; measuring and cooking spoons retain the general spoon ancestor.
A spoon intended for preparing food, including stirring. Neither wood nor metal is required.
A kitchen tool for measuring ingredient volume. Include fixed-capacity dry cups as well as graduated liquid cups; not a drinking-glass material sense or a numerical cup unit.
A spoon-shaped kitchen tool for measuring ingredient volume. A measuring utensil is distinct from a spoonful amount or a jurisdiction-specific tablespoon unit.
A bowl used when mixing ingredients by hand or machine; do not require an electric mixer.
A board used as a support while cutting food. Manufacturer polypropylene boards disprove a wood-only definition.
A kitchen tool for sifting food material through apertures. Exclude analytic screening and computer-display senses.
A kitchen sieve intended for sifting flour; no crank, trigger mechanism or metal material is mandatory.
A mesh kitchen strainer used to separate larger food particles from liquid. Do not identify it with every colander or all dry sieves.
A kitchen implement for turning or lifting food. Do not import the dictionary broad cookware genus into the narrower vessel family.
A kitchen spatula used to mix or spread food; this is a food-use restriction of the wider hand-tool sense.
Tongs intended for taking hold of food. Pointed hooks, a separate hinge and one particular material are not universal.
A vessel used with a pestle to crush, grind or mix food. Exclude artillery, masonry mortar, and a claim that every mortar comes with a pestle.
A hand tool used to grind or crush food in a mortar. Exclude the ore-stamping machine and slab-grinding implement senses.
Mixing food materials during preparation. The existing general mixing concept remains broader than food work.
Stirring food material with an implement or mixer; not emotional agitation or mixing abstract ideas.
Vigorous beating used when preparing food. The existing Russian action is broader and also covers fluffing nonfood objects.
Reducing food to smaller pieces or particles; do not restrict the general comminution anchor to food or to just one mechanism.
Reducing food by crushing, pounding or abrasion. Not the sound, dance, monotonous-work or particle-size noun senses.
Passing flour through a sieve to separate coarser material or lumps. Do not equate this with the dictionary noun for winnowing chaff.
Bread browned or crisped by heating. Exclude a drinking salutation, celebrated person and slang doomed-person meaning.
Browning or crisping bread through heat, including an electric toaster. This is not pan frying and need not use an open fire.
Removing unwanted dirt or contamination from physical objects. This broad physical process includes household and shoe cleaning; no disinfection or guaranteed cleanliness is asserted.
Removing dirt from footwear, distinct from removing the peel of food.
A brush intended for physical cleaning. This purpose is not imposed on every brush, including brushes used to apply substances.
A brush specifically used to remove dirt from footwear; do not make shoe polish or a particular bristle material mandatory.
A brush used for vigorous surface cleaning. Keep it narrower than the general cleaning-brush family.
Physical stirring, including mechanical agitation, not metaphorical excitement.
Keep the Russian process broad enough for pillows and food; use a composed English label and put culinary whipping in a separate subtype.
Physical reduction to smaller pieces; the Russian dictionary includes grain, rock and ore, so do not restrict the anchor to food.
Physical sieving, excluding analytic selection. Retain the proseyaniye variant pending historical usage review.
Heat treatment of a liquid; preserve the existing water-boiling child and distinguish cooking by boiling. The uncertain shorter kipyatenie variant is deferred.
Physical rubbing, broader than food grinding and distinct from a copied drawing made by rubbing.
The action of causing liquid to flow; not emotion, rain, or a crowd moving.
Physically changing which side of an object faces outward or upward; not communication, business turnover, or deliberation.
Retain the household context; broad physical cleaning is a separate parent, and harvesting is excluded.
Remove the wrong Russian verb meaning make someone laugh, which was tagged as English; preserve genuine mixing forms.
Reuse kitchen tool/utensil; no duplicate general kitchen-utensil node.
Reuse colander; do not make every colander a fine-mesh strainer.
Reuse culinary whisk; do not import the clothes-brush homonym or universal wire-material requirement.
Reuse grater and add a food-specific purpose.
Reuse rolling pin and its dough-rolling purpose; do not copy the wood-and-two-handles gloss as a universal condition.
Reuse toaster; distinguish the appliance from the person proposing a toast.
Retain the food-peeling identity and move unrelated shoe/brush assertions.
Retain household cleaning and qualify English lookup; broad physical cleaning is a separate genus.
Laboratory volumetric ware is not a genus of ordinary kitchen measuring utensils.
Defer the malformed preparation record until its general-preparation versus cooking senses are reviewed; do not guess a cooking duplicate merge.
Physical seizing has misplaced poke/insert synonyms; defer that cohort rather than attach a new kitchen tool to the contaminated record.
Do not use the winnowing noun as a synonym of every sieve-based separation.
A spoonful quantity is not the spoon utensil or volume-measuring instrument.
Artillery mortar is not a kitchen vessel.
Masonry mortar is not a kitchen vessel.
An ore-stamping machine is not the kitchen hand pestle.

review.limits: A bounded utensil and process cohort, not a complete kitchen or cleaning ontology. Broad dishware containment/purpose assertions, other cooking methods, cooking/food terminology, generic filter/sieve genera, fork/knife/glass material claims, physical grasping duplicates and the ambiguous generated preparation record 6411 need further review. The Russian variants proseyaniye and kipyateniye are retained pending separate historical/usage review; obvious doubled-suffix artifacts are removed. No culinary conversions, food safety rules, product recommendations or application test suites.

refreshed_comparison.caveat: Exact normalized English spellings are candidates, not semantic identities or a missing-concept count.
